newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark says it backs EU defence against U.S. law.
newsitem.headline: Denmark says it backs EU defence against U.S. law.

text.p: Denmark says it issued a threat to veto a European Union counterattack over Washington's anti-Cuba trade laws because of the method chosen by the EU and attempts were being made to find a different approach.
Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen told the news agency Ritzau that Denmark did not in principle oppose the EU stance against Washington's Helms-Burton Act.

"Denmark is not against the European Union taking precautionary measures against the U.S.A. -- it's just that we cannot accept the use of Article 235 (of the EU's founding Treaty of Rome)," he said in the report carried overnight.
"I know that others are trying to find an alternative basis on which to proceed."

EU efforts to combat the Helms-Burton Act, an amalgamation of years of anti-Cuba policy, were thrown into turmoil on Tuesday when Denmark said it would veto proposed retaliatory measures under Article 235.
The article allows the EU to act in policy areas not specified elsewhere in the treaty and is regarded with suspicion by governments wary of ceding too much authority to the bloc.

The 14 other EU member states have accepted the use of Article 235 over the Helms-Burton Act. But diplomats say Denmark has been made especially sensitive to issues of sovereignty by a pending court case on the issue.

"It's surely no coincidence that Denmark, which has approved the use of this article more than once in the past, now sees it as a possible challenge to sovereign powers while Britain, a country that is generally the first to sound the alarm, has no objections," a European Union diplomat said.

EU foreign ministers are due to discuss proposals that would allow countersuits to be brought anywhere in Europe against litigants who sue European companies or individuals for contravening the Helms-Burton Act, whose practical implications have been suspended until January.

Among other things the act allows naturalised Americans to take action in U.S. courts against "traffickers" -- foreign companies or individuals accused of gaining from investments made in property confiscated in Cuba since the 1959 Communist revolution.

In Denmark, a group of 11 citizens has filed a suit saying the government's signature of the EU Maastricht treaty contravenes the country's constitution by transferring too much political and judicial authority to supranational institutions.
Danish officials deny that the veto threat has any connection with the court case -- preliminary hearings begin next week -- and say it is because Article 235 has become outdated.

"It has nothing to do with the Supreme Court's examination of the constitutional case. It is because the Maastricht agreement is far more precise on matters of authority than was the Treaty of Rome," Ove Fich, chairman of the Danish parliament's Europe committee, told Ritzau.
But European diplomats are sceptical. One said: "Definitely it is a political problem relating to the court judgment.
"They are more than cautious about anything which could relate to this judgment and Paragraph 235 is, of course, part of this whole discussion."

While Denmark's Social Democrat-led government is publicly pro-EU, its members have varying degrees of reservations. The public, which rocked the EU by rejecting Maastricht in a 1992 referendum, is decidely lukewarm.

Although the electorate grudgingly approved the accord in a 1993 plebiscite, it did so only on condition that Denmark stay out of Economic and Monetary Union and reject other clauses seen as a danger to national independence.
